faq.q: Why does a fast train have to push so much air?
faq.a: At 300 kilometres per hour a train sweeps through more than 80 metres of air every second, and all of it has to be shoved aside and closed up behind.
asks: How much air does a train push?

faq.q: Why does air resistance grow so fast with speed?
faq.a: The faster you go, the more air you hit each second and the harder you hit it. Together that makes drag grow with the square of speed, so twice as fast means about four times the drag.
asks: Why is drag worse at high speed?

faq.a: When a fast train enters a tunnel, its nose squeezes the air ahead into a pressure wave that travels down the tunnel and bursts out of the far end with a bang. Long pointed noses make the wave weaker.
asks: Why do trains make a bang in tunnels?

faq.q: Why was a train nose shaped like a kingfisher?
faq.a: The kingfisher dives from air into much denser water with hardly a splash, thanks to its long tapered beak. Engineer Eiji Nakatsu used that idea for the 500 Series Shinkansen nose to cut the tunnel boom.

faq.q: Why don't slow trains need pointed noses?
faq.a: At low speed air resistance is small, so a blunt front wastes little energy, and a flatter front gives more room for passengers and the driver.
asks: Why are some trains flat at the front?

facts: The nose of the 500 Series Shinkansen was inspired by the kingfisher's beak.
Air resistance grows with the square of speed.
Tunnel boom happens when a pressure wave pushed ahead of a train bursts out of the tunnel exit.
